Day-ahead forecasting of French electricity consumption

Can we beat RTE’s public forecast? Full report of the project

Authors

Léo Bouchand

Nicolas Le Jeune

Published

October 20, 2026

In one sentence. We don’t beat RTE without its forecast, we beat it by correcting it: our final model cuts RTE’s error by 37 % on the test year, and a simple hourly debiasing rule by 43 %.

1 Executive summary

Every day D before 12:00, a utility’s trading desk buys on the day-ahead market the energy of each hour of D+1. It needs a forecast of the 24 hours of tomorrow, made only with what is known at noon. RTE, the French grid operator, publishes such a forecast for free: it is the benchmark to beat. The manager asked three questions.

The manager’s three questions
Question Answer
1. Can we do better than RTE, and by how much? Yes, by correcting RTE’s forecast. Our final model (LightGBM on RTE’s residual) has an MAE of 910 MW against 1,439 MW for RTE (-36.8 %). A simple rule, RTE minus its recent bias at the same hour, does even better: 819 MW (-43.1 %).
2. How uncertain is it, and when does it fail? The 80 % and 95 % bands are about 2.4 GW and 4.2 GW wide. They hold 76 % and 94 % of test hours, but only 51 % and 73 % on cold evening peaks. The model fails when RTE fails: Christmas week, holidays, cold days, some weekends.
3. What should we deploy, and what are the risks? The LightGBM residual now (chosen by a rule fixed before the test, with uncertainty bands), and the hourly debiasing rule alongside it as a candidate. Main risk: RTE’s forecast must be published before noon, which is not verified yet.

2 The problem and the rules of the game

  • Cutoff. The forecast is sent on D at 12:00, Paris time. Consumption is known up to D 11:00, so for a target day T = D+1 the last complete day is T-2. Every feature has a lag of 48 hours or more.
  • Target. The 24 hourly loads of D+1, i.e. 12 to 36 hours ahead.
  • Test year. 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026 (8,760 hours). It is only used to report. Every choice (training period, hyperparameters, final model) is made on 4 quarterly walk-forward folds, July 2024 to June 2025.
  • Metric. MAE in MW on three scopes: all hours, the evening peak (18:00-21:00, the most expensive hours) and the evening peak of cold days (daily mean temperature below 5 °C, 81 hours on 27 days).
  • Temperature. The dataset holds the observed temperature, not a weather forecast. Using the temperature of D+1 would mean a perfect weather forecast, so we use the temperature of T-2 (“persistence”) and only show the observed one as an upper bound.
  • Data. Hourly national consumption from 01 January 2019 to 30 June 2026 (65,710 hours), with temperature and RTE’s day-ahead forecast. Only 7 RTE values are missing (one per year, at the autumn clock change).

3 What we forecast

Exploration (notebook 00_eda) shows:

  • Three seasonalities. Daily (low at night, peaks in the morning and at 19:00 in winter), weekly (weekends are much lower during the day) and yearly (winter days are almost twice summer days). STL gives a seasonal strength of 0.81 for the week and 0.90 for the year.
  • The cold drives the level. Below about 15 °C each degree less adds roughly 2 GW (heating); above, the load is flat with a small rise in heat waves. Temperature is the key variable, but D+1’s temperature is unknown at the cutoff.
  • Usable lags. Only 48 h and 168 h are available at the cutoff; both have an autocorrelation around 0.9.
  • Stationarity. ADF and KPSS find no unit root on the daily series, but the 2022-2023 drop (energy crisis, sobriety) makes the choice of training years important.

4 The benchmark: RTE is good but too low

RTE’s forecast is accurate (MAPE 2.9 % on the test year) but it has been too low by about 1.1 GW since 2023: it did not follow the lower post-crisis consumption. On the test year its bias is -1,086 MW and it depends on the hour. A systematic error can be corrected: this is the observation the whole project turns on.

5 Our path: from naive baselines to correcting RTE

We followed the course milestones, each notebook with the same layout (verdict, setup, model, results, where it fails, conclusion, appendix).

5.1 Naive baselines (01_baseline)

Same hour one week before (lag 7d) and two days before (lag 2d). Both are more than twice RTE’s error. Lag 7d breaks on cold days and weather changes (9.2 GW of MAE on cold evening peaks, since it copies a milder week); lag 2d breaks when the copied day is of another type (Sunday for Tuesday).

5.2 Classical daily models (02_ar, 03_sarima)

On the daily mean, trained on 2023 to mid-2025:

  • AR(8) on the anomaly. Consumption = a seasonal normal (2 Fourier pairs + one level per weekday) + an anomaly, modelled as an AR(p). The PACF rule and the AIC both give p = 8.
  • SARIMA(2,0,2)(0,1,1)7 and Holt-Winters (additive weekly season, damped trend). Both boil down to a fixed weekly profile on a very persistent level.
  • SARIMAX with heating and cooling degrees and holidays, as a regression with SARIMA errors: each heating degree adds 0.75 GW, a holiday removes 3.8 GW.

None of them beats RTE. They react to cold spells about two days late, and even with a perfect weather forecast the SARIMAX only matches RTE.

5.3 Hourly LightGBM (04_lightgbm)

One gradient boosting model for the 24 hours of D+1, with lags of 48 h and more, rolling means, calendar, holidays and the T-2 temperature. A perturbation test (add 10 GW at hour s, the first changed feature row must be s + 48) checks the cutoff. Starting the training in 2019 beats 2023 on every fold, and hyperparameters matter much less.

  • Without RTE, our best honest model reaches 2,010 MW, 40 % worse than RTE. Only the upper bound with observed temperature beats it.
  • With RTE’s forecast as a feature, LightGBM gets 908 MW. RTE’s forecast takes 99 % of the gain: the model is really a per-hour correction of RTE. But trees cannot extrapolate, so peaks are cut (85 GW for an actual 90 GW).

5.4 Final model: LightGBM on RTE’s residual (05_final_model)

The target becomes load - RTE, and the forecast is RTE + learnt correction. The peaks come from RTE, no extrapolation is needed. On the folds it ties with LightGBM + RTE (860 MW each, 0.09 % apart); the rule fixed beforehand (best mean, then best on cold evening peaks if within 1 %) picks the residual model (1,478 vs 1,557 MW on cold evening peaks). Prediction intervals are split conformal: per-hour quantiles of the validation errors.

5.5 Extension: debiasing RTE’s forecast (extension_rte_debiased)

No training at all: RTE minus its mean error at the same local hour over the 28 days T-29 to T-2. It is the best on the folds (830 MW vs 860 MW) and on the test. A flat correction (same for every hour) is not enough: RTE’s bias depends on the hour.

6 Q1. Can we beat RTE? Yes, on every scope

Both corrected forecasts beat RTE on all hours, on the evening peak and on the cold evening peaks that cost the most: 17 % lower error there for the final model, 34 % for the debiasing rule. The same order holds on the walk-forward folds (830 MW, 860 MW and 1,362 MW), so the result is not an artefact of the test year.

WarningToo good to be true?

Beating the benchmark by a third is a bug until proven otherwise. We checked: lags of 48 h or more everywhere (perturbation test), chronological splits, nothing tuned on the test. The gain comes from a real, large and hour-dependent bias of RTE. Two caveats remain: RTE’s publication time is assumed, not verified, and we used consolidated data rather than the real-time vintage available at noon.

7 Q2. How uncertain, and when does it fail?

7.1 On a cold week, the model misses the same days as RTE

The final model reaches the peaks (90.0 GW for an actual 90.2 GW) but misses whole days when RTE does. On the 15 worst days of the test year, the final model and RTE err in the same direction: Christmas week, holidays (1 November on a Saturday), cold days (21 November, 5 January), some weekends and Mondays. The model removes RTE’s usual error, not its error of the day.

7.2 The 80 % band holds on average, not in the cold

The width depends only on the hour, not on season or temperature, so the band is narrowest where errors cost the most. Conditioning on “cold at the cutoff” (T-2 below 5 °C) only lifts the 80 % coverage on cold days from 55 % to 65 %. A safety margin, or regimes based on RTE’s forecast level, would probably work better.

7.3 Errors grow in the cold, but the model beats RTE at every temperature

The error roughly doubles below 5 °C compared with mild days, and these days are rare (27 in the test year, 3 below 0 °C). Cold evening peaks are 0.9 % of hours but 1.9 % of the final model’s error volume, and imbalance prices are highest there.

8 Q3. What to deploy, and the risks

Recommendation. Deploy the LightGBM residual (05): it was chosen by a rule fixed before the test and it comes with prediction intervals. Run the hourly debiasing rule alongside it as a candidate: it is simpler and better on average (819 MW vs 910 MW), but it was added after the selection rule of 05 and has no uncertainty band yet. Fallbacks: RTE raw if our model breaks, the LightGBM without RTE (2,010 MW) if RTE is late.

Deployment risks
Risk Impact Mitigation
RTE’s forecast arrives after noon (assumed, not verified) Both corrected forecasts need it Check RTE’s publication calendar; fall back to the LightGBM without RTE
RTE’s bias changes suddenly The rule takes about a month (28-day window) to follow; the LightGBM until retraining Monitor the 7-day bias, alert beyond ±0.5 GW, retrain regularly
Live data differ from the consolidated data we tested on Live error higher than measured Replay the model on archived real-time data before go-live
Extreme cold and unusual holidays Worst days; the 80 % band only holds 51 % of cold evening peaks Manual override and a wider safety margin on cold days and around holidays

9 Limits and next steps

  • Weather forecast. With the observed temperature as an upper bound, LightGBM without RTE reaches 1,184 MW: a real weather forecast is the main lever to become independent from RTE.
  • Intervals in the cold. Make the conformal bands depend on a regime known at the cutoff (RTE’s forecast level, forecast temperature), or add a fixed margin on cold days.
  • Intervals for the debiasing rule. The same split conformal method applies directly to its errors.
  • Real-time data. Re-run the evaluation on the real-time vintage before trusting the measured gains.

10 Appendix

10.1 Definitions

  • MAE (mean absolute error): average of |forecast - actual| over the hours of a scope, in MW. Lower is better. “vs RTE raw” is the relative gap to RTE’s MAE.
  • Bias: average of (forecast - actual). Negative means the forecast is too low.
  • Walk-forward validation: train on the past, test on the next quarter, 4 times (July 2024 to June 2025).
  • Coverage: share of test hours where the actual load falls inside the prediction interval.

10.2 Reproducibility

The numbers of this report are computed at render time from the test forecasts saved in data/predictions/ (code/report_data.py), and the figures come from code/07_executive_summary.ipynb. To rebuild it, run the notebooks 01 to 05, the extension and 07, then from reports/:

quarto render            # output/report.html and output/one_pager.pdf

00_eda exploration of the series and of RTE’s error
01_baseline naive baselines vs RTE
02_ar, 03_sarima daily models: AR, SARIMA, Holt-Winters, SARIMAX
04_lightgbm hourly LightGBM, walk-forward
